narrative:
The model determined that you have a 90.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and wants to admit students likely to succeed, this strong prediction of failure led to your application being rejected.

Three factors drove this decision, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction heavily toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) in your third year, compared to an average of about 5.8 among accepted students, signaled to the model that you struggled significantly in later law school coursework. 

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. At 25.5, it sits well below the 37.2 average of admitted students, indicating the model saw this as a key indicator of difficulty passing the bar.

Your first-year class ranking came third. Like your third-year rank, being in the lowest decile (1 versus an average of 6 among accepted students) further reinforced the outlook of future struggles.

Taken together, these academic performance signals were strong enough that the model concluded you were very likely to fail the bar exam, making admission too risky for the school.

What you should do next is focus on improving your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Strengthening these areas will directly address the factors that led to this outcome and improve your chances in future applications. (248 words)
